claims.text: Motivation is the willingness of a person to put effort into their work, and the set of reasons behind that willingness. A motivated employee directs effort towards what the job requires because something about the work or its rewards makes doing so worthwhile to them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour differs from the other inputs a business buys because the output it produces depends on willingness as well as on quantity. A machine hired for eight hours delivers eight hours of capacity; an employee paid for eight hours delivers somewhere between the minimum that avoids trouble and the most they are capable of, and where in that range they work is what motivation decides.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Motivation reaches business objectives through several separate channels, and each has its own measure: productivity, which is output per employee per period; absenteeism, the working days lost to unplanned absence; labour turnover, the proportion of the workforce leaving and needing replacement; the quality of work, measured by reject, rework or complaint rates; and the number of usable improvement ideas employees bring forward. A motivation method may move one of these and leave the others where they were.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Higher productivity lowers the labour cost of each unit of output, because the same wage bill is spread over more units. If a workshop paying N$96 000 a month in wages produces 4 000 units, labour costs N$24 a unit; at 4 800 units the same wage bill costs N$20 a unit. Where the business can sell the extra output, or use the freed hours, that N$4 saving per unit widens the gap between price and cost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Replacing an employee who leaves costs the business the money spent on advertising and selecting a replacement, the cost of training them, and the output lost while the new person is still learning the job. These costs are incurred each time a post turns over, so a business with persistently high labour turnover pays them repeatedly for the same post.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The objectives motivation serves depend on what the organisation exists to do. A private firm may be pursuing survival, profit, growth or market share; a state-owned utility or a hospital may be pursuing service targets and cost control without any profit objective at all. In each situation the link runs the same way: employee effort determines how much of the work gets done, and to what standard.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Willingness raises output where the employee also has the skill, the equipment, the materials and the authority to act on it. A motivated machinist with a broken machine produces nothing, and a motivated clerk who has to refer every decision upwards is held at the speed of the person above. Motivation is one determinant of productivity among several, so a business that raises motivation and leaves the others untouched may see little change.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Satisfaction and motivation are not the same thing. A contented employee may be comfortable precisely because the work asks little of them, and a highly motivated one may be dissatisfied with pay or conditions while still working hard at a task they care about. A business measuring only how happy its staff say they are has not measured effort.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A human need is something a person requires or strongly desires, whose absence creates a tension the person acts to remove. The action a person takes to remove that tension is what an employer sees as behaviour at work.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An unmet need directs behaviour towards meeting it, and the stronger the need, the more of a person's attention and effort it takes. Once a need has been largely met it tends to lose its power to direct behaviour, and another need takes over as the one that presses hardest. This is why a reward that changed someone's behaviour last year may do little this year.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Human needs run from the physical requirements of staying alive - food, water, warmth, shelter, rest - through the need to feel safe and secure, the need to belong and be accepted by others, the need to be respected and to think well of oneself, and the need to grow and use one's abilities fully. Which of these presses hardest differs between people and changes over a person's life.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A need in this sense is a requirement a person acts to satisfy; a want is a preference about how to satisfy it. Two employees may share the same need for security and want quite different things - one a permanent contract, the other a medical aid scheme for a family member. Employers work with wants because those are what can be offered, but it is the underlying need that explains why the offer changes behaviour.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Work satisfies human needs by two different routes, and it helps to keep them apart. Pay satisfies needs indirectly: the money itself meets nothing, but it buys food, housing, transport and school fees, and it can be saved against future trouble. The job satisfies other needs directly: the company of colleagues, the standing that comes with a role, the interest of the work and the sense of having done something well are received at work and cannot be bought elsewhere with the same wage.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Particular features of a job answer particular needs. Wages and a guaranteed minimum of hours answer physical needs. A permanent contract, safe conditions, sick pay and a pension answer the need for security. Working alongside others, team tasks and social facilities answer the need to belong. A job title, recognition and promotion answer the need for respect. Difficult work, training, responsibility and the freedom to decide how to do the job answer the need to grow.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Work may fail to meet needs in ways that match the same list. Pay below what local prices require leaves physical needs unmet; short or casual contracts and unsafe conditions leave security needs unmet; isolated or heavily supervised work leaves social needs unmet; work whose results go unnoticed leaves the need for respect unmet; and a job that repeats one narrow task with no route out leaves the need to grow unmet. A job may meet some of these well and others not at all.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The same job meets needs differently for different employees, because each arrives with a different need pressing hardest. A student working weekends at a lodge may value flexible hours and the company of other young staff and care little about a pension; a parent supporting a household from the same job may value the guaranteed hours and the medical aid above everything else. A single reward offered to both will therefore change one person's behaviour more than the other's.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Work is not the only place needs are met. An employee may meet social needs through family, church or sport, and meet the need to use their abilities through something they do outside working hours. Where that is so, the same workplace reward - a social club, a demanding project - carries less weight for them than for someone whose main source of company or challenge is the job.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Raising pay is not the same as meeting all of an employee's needs. Money answers the needs that can be bought and leaves untouched the need to be respected, to belong and to grow, which is why a business can raise wages and still find its most capable staff leaving for work that interests them more.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The theories in this topic answer two different questions. A content theory asks what it is that motivates people - which needs or rewards make effort worthwhile - and Taylor, Mayo, Maslow, Herzberg and McClelland are all content theories. A process theory asks how motivation comes about - the thinking that turns a reward on offer into effort actually given - and Vroom's expectancy theory is the process theory named in this syllabus.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The six theories disagree about what money does. For Taylor it is the main lever, provided pay is tied to measured output. For Mayo it matters, but social belonging and the attention of managers matter as well. For Maslow it answers the lower levels of the hierarchy and loses force once those are met. For Herzberg it is a hygiene factor whose absence causes dissatisfaction while its presence does not by itself produce positive motivation. For McClelland it is one reward among three, and it suits someone driven by achievement only where it is read as a score. For Vroom money motivates where the employee believes the target is reachable, believes the payment will follow, and values the money more than the effort it costs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each of these theories was developed from a particular workforce at a particular time - Taylor from steelworks labouring, Mayo from an American factory in the 1920s and 1930s, Herzberg from interviews with professional staff. How useful a theory is in a given business depends on how closely that business resembles the setting the theory came from, which is why applying one of them to a modern service business calls for judgement rather than transfer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: In practice the theories are used together rather than chosen between. A business may take from Herzberg the instruction to correct pay and conditions before expecting enthusiasm, from Mayo and Maslow the case for team working and belonging, from McClelland the idea of matching tasks to what an individual is driven by, and from Vroom a test of whether the reward chain it has built actually holds together.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Taylor's scientific management holds that work should be studied and measured rather than left to custom, that there is one most efficient way to perform any manual task, and that employees are motivated mainly by money, so pay should be tied directly to measured output.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The method Taylor set out runs in order: observe and time how the task is done at present; break it into its simple repeated elements and identify the quickest sound way to perform each; set a standard output from that; select employees suited to the task and train them to the one method; then pay a piece rate that rewards output above the standard and supervise closely to see the method is followed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where a task is repetitive and its output can be counted and checked, Taylor's approach can raise output quickly, because the employee's earnings rise with the number of units produced and the method has been simplified so that producing more is possible. It also makes the labour cost of each unit predictable for the business, since pay moves with output rather than with hours.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The approach has serious limits. It treats employees as instruments rather than people, so it takes no account of the need to belong, to be respected or to grow. It assumes money dominates, which holds better where pay is low relative to living costs than where it is not. Paying for speed can pull quality down unless inspection is added, which costs money in its turn. Repetitive simplified work is associated with boredom and resentment, and the approach does not fit work whose output cannot be counted, such as nursing, teaching or design.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Mayo's conclusions came from the Hawthorne studies, carried out at an American electrical factory between 1924 and 1932. Groups of employees were observed while working conditions such as lighting, rest breaks and hours were varied. Output rose under several different changes, and in some groups it stayed high when conditions were returned to what they had been, so the physical changes alone did not explain the results.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Mayo's human relations school holds that employees are motivated by social needs as well as by pay: by belonging to a working group, by the attention and interest of managers, and by having a say in how their work is arranged. Work groups develop their own standards of what a fair day's output is, and those group standards influence individual effort.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The practical measures that follow from Mayo are organising work in teams rather than isolating individuals, consulting employees about changes that affect them, giving managers a role in listening as well as directing, providing places and occasions for employees to mix, and paying attention to the informal groups that form rather than only to the formal structure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Group norms cut both ways: a group that decides a certain output is enough may hold back its faster members as firmly as it pulls up its slower ones, so team working can restrict output as well as raise it. The Hawthorne studies also rested on small numbers of employees in one factory in one country, and the interpretation of what caused the changes has been disputed ever since, so the findings are better treated as a reason to take social needs seriously than as a measured rule.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Maslow's hierarchy of needs arranges human needs in five levels, drawn as a pyramid with the most basic at the bottom: physiological needs such as food, water and rest; safety needs, meaning security and freedom from danger; love and belonging, meaning acceptance by a group; esteem, meaning respect from others and self-respect; and self-actualisation, meaning the full use of a person's abilities.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The rule that makes the hierarchy a theory of motivation is that a level becomes a motivator once the levels below it are largely satisfied, and that a need which has been satisfied loses its power to motivate. On this view, offering more of what an employee already has enough of changes little, while offering the level they have not yet reached can change a great deal.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Applied at work, the hierarchy tells a manager to identify the level an employee has reached and offer the reward that matches it: adequate wages and rest breaks for physiological needs; a permanent contract, safe conditions and a pension for safety needs; team work and social occasions for belonging; job titles, recognition and promotion for esteem; and demanding work, training and the freedom to decide how to do the job for self-actualisation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The hierarchy is hard to use precisely. There is no reliable way to tell which level an employee has reached, so the diagnosis is a judgement. Not everyone moves up in the stated order - an artist or an entrepreneur may pursue self-fulfilment while security is still uncertain. Self-actualisation has no measure, so a business cannot tell whether it has provided it. And a single reward often answers several levels at once: a pay rise can meet safety needs and, where it is publicly awarded, esteem as well.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A supermarket chain in Windhoek finds that its shelf-fillers, who are paid above the local going rate on permanent contracts, respond very little to a further wage offer, while its longest-serving supervisors, on the same terms, are leaving. Read through the hierarchy, the shelf-fillers' physiological and safety needs are largely met, so more money adds little, and belonging or esteem is the level to work on. The supervisors' complaint is that they have nowhere further to go, which points to esteem and self-actualisation rather than pay.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Herzberg's two-factor theory separates the things at work that cause dissatisfaction when they are wrong from the things that produce positive motivation when they are present. The first group he called hygiene factors, or maintenance factors; the second group he called motivators.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Herzberg's hygiene factors are pay, working conditions, company policy and administration, the quality of supervision, job security and relationships with colleagues. Getting them wrong causes dissatisfaction. Putting them right removes that dissatisfaction, which is not the same as producing enthusiasm - on this theory, correcting them brings an employee to neutral rather than to positive effort.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Herzberg's motivators are achievement, recognition for achievement, the nature of the work itself, responsibility, advancement and personal growth. These arise from what the employee does rather than from the conditions surrounding it, which is why the theory points a business towards changing the content of jobs rather than only improving the surroundings.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The claim that gives the theory its force is that satisfaction and dissatisfaction are not two ends of one scale but two separate scales. The opposite of dissatisfaction is no dissatisfaction, not motivation. It follows that a business which fixes canteen, conditions and pay and then finds effort unchanged has not failed to spend enough; it has spent on the wrong scale.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Herzberg's practical prescription is job enrichment: give the employee a complete and identifiable piece of work rather than a fragment, the authority and responsibility to decide how it is done, and direct feedback on the result, so that achievement, responsibility and growth are built into the job itself. He distinguished this from simply adding more tasks of the same kind, which he regarded as changing the quantity of work rather than its quality.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The evidence came from interviews with around two hundred professional employees, mostly accountants and engineers, so extending the findings to manual, casual or low-paid work is uncertain. The interview method invited people to attribute good episodes to themselves and bad ones to their surroundings, which may have produced the split rather than discovered it. And the line between the two lists is not clean: where pay is below what an employee needs to live on, pay behaves like a motivator, and pay awarded publicly for an achievement carries recognition with it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: McClelland's acquired needs theory holds that three needs shape behaviour at work: the need for achievement, the need for affiliation and the need for power. He called them acquired because he held that they are learned through a person's experience and culture rather than being present from birth, and that the strength of each differs from person to person.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A person in whom the need for achievement is strong looks for goals that are demanding but reachable, wants personal responsibility for the result and wants concrete feedback on how they did; the accomplishment matters to them more than the reward attached to it. A person in whom the need for affiliation is strong wants to be accepted and to keep relationships harmonious, and works well where cooperation matters. A person in whom the need for power is strong wants influence over outcomes and over other people.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: All three needs are present in each person in some combination, so the theory is about which is dominant rather than about sorting people into types. The dominant need shapes both what motivates the person and the roles they are likely to do well in: a strongly achievement-driven employee may be an excellent individual performer and an impatient manager, while a manager who seeks influence for the sake of the organisation rather than for personal standing may be more effective at directing others.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Applied at work, the theory tells a manager to match tasks and rewards to what drives the individual: a stretching individual target with quick, specific feedback for someone driven by achievement; a team role, mentoring or customer contact for someone driven by affiliation; and responsibility for a project, a budget or a group of staff for someone driven by influence.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Identifying which need dominates in a particular employee is difficult and the judgement is subjective, so a manager may assign work on a misreading. The dominant need can also change as a person's circumstances change, so a diagnosis made once may not hold. And a small business may have no role available that matches what an employee is driven by, in which case the theory diagnoses a problem it cannot solve.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Vroom's expectancy theory is a process theory: rather than listing what people want, it explains how an employee decides how much effort to give. It holds that a person puts in effort when they expect that effort to produce the performance required, expect that performance to be rewarded, and place value on the reward offered.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The three elements are expectancy, instrumentality and valence. Expectancy is the employee's belief that their effort will actually produce the required level of performance. Instrumentality is their belief that reaching that performance will actually bring the reward. Valence is how much the employee values that particular reward.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The three elements combine by multiplication rather than addition: motivational force = expectancy x instrumentality x valence, with each element treated as a figure between 0 and 1. The consequence of multiplying is that a near-zero value on any one element pulls the whole result to near zero, so a generous reward the employee has no expectation of reaching motivates almost nothing, and a reachable, reliably paid reward the employee does not want motivates almost nothing either.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: To use the theory on a reward scheme, test the three links separately. Ask whether the target is reachable by an employee working hard, given their training and equipment - if it is not, raise expectancy by adjusting the target or the training. Ask whether the reward reliably follows the performance and whether the employee can see the connection - if not, raise instrumentality by making the rule explicit and paying it when it is earned. Ask whether the reward is one the employee values - if not, raise valence by offering something they do.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The three elements are beliefs held inside an employee's head, so a business cannot measure them directly and has to infer them from what people say and do. The theory also assumes a fairly deliberate weighing-up, which fits a decision about whether to chase an annual bonus better than it fits day-to-day effort. It explains how a reward works without saying which rewards people value, so it is normally used alongside a content theory rather than instead of one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A logistics firm in Walvis Bay offers its drivers a monthly bonus of N$3 000 for a delivery record with no late loads. Drivers believe the target is reachable in perhaps eight months out of ten, and the yard's scheduling is the reason for the other two, so expectancy is about 0.8. The bonus has been paid whenever it was earned, so instrumentality is about 0.9. Drivers value the money highly, so valence is about 0.7. Multiplying gives 0.8 x 0.9 = 0.72, and 0.72 x 0.7 = 0.504 - a scheme with real pull. If the yard's scheduling worsened so that drivers thought the target reachable only three months in ten, expectancy would fall to about 0.3 and the same N$3 000 would carry a force of about 0.19, because 0.3 x 0.9 = 0.27 and 0.27 x 0.7 = 0.189.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Using a motivation theory in a real business runs in a set order. Establish what the actual problem is and how it shows up in the figures - absence, turnover, output per employee, reject rates, complaints. Work out which need that evidence points to as unmet. Choose the method that answers that need and that the business can afford. Then check the reward chain: whether the target is reachable, whether the reward follows reliably, and whether the employees concerned value it. Finally, decide in advance which figure will show whether it worked.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The same motivation problem calls for different answers in different businesses, because the facts change what will work. A small enterprise with six employees cannot offer a promotion ladder, so it reaches esteem needs through recognition, responsibility and job titles instead. A business paying close to the legal minimum in a high-cost town is dealing with an unmet physiological need, so enriching jobs before correcting pay is likely to change little. A business whose work is done in isolation has a social need to answer that a business built on teams does not.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A theory developed in one setting may fit another badly. Herzberg's separation of pay from motivation came from professional employees whose pay already covered their needs comfortably, and it holds less well among employees for whom the wage decides whether the household eats. Taylor's piece rates assume output that can be counted and checked, which excludes much service and professional work. Judging the fit before applying the theory is part of applying it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A motivation measure is judged by what changes after it, so the figure to watch is chosen before the measure is introduced and read again afterwards. Absence days, labour turnover, output per employee per shift, reject rates and customer complaints are all measurable. Where the figure does not move, the business has learned that the need it diagnosed was not the binding one, which is information rather than waste.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Financial and non-financial methods are normally used together rather than chosen between, because they answer different needs. Pay at a level the employee regards as fair removes a source of dissatisfaction and makes the rest possible; responsibility, recognition and development supply the reasons to give more than the minimum. A business that offers only one of the two is likely to find that raising it further brings progressively less in return.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A payment method is the rule a business uses to turn an employee's time, output or results into the money it pays them. The methods named in this syllabus are time-based pay, salary, piece rates, commission, bonuses, profit sharing, performance-related pay and fringe benefits.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Payment methods differ chiefly in how tightly pay is tied to something measured. Time-based pay and salary tie pay to attendance; piece rates, commission and performance-related pay tie it to a measured result; bonuses and profit sharing tie part of it to an outcome reached later. The tighter the tie, the stronger the incentive to move the measured quantity - and the greater the risk that the parts of the job which are not measured, such as care, safety and helping colleagues, receive less attention.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Most businesses combine methods rather than relying on one. A basic wage or salary gives the employee the security of a predictable income and the employer a workforce that turns up; a variable element on top - commission, a bonus, a performance award - supplies the incentive. The proportions can be adjusted, and moving more of the pay into the variable part shifts risk from the employer to the employee.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Time-based pay, also called a time rate, pays an employee an agreed amount for each hour or day worked, so gross pay = hours worked x rate per hour. Hours beyond the standard working week are often paid at a higher overtime rate.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A Windhoek joinery pays its bench hands N$28 an hour for a 40-hour week and time-and-a-half for overtime. In a week with 6 hours of overtime the basic pay is 40 x N$28 = N$1 120. The overtime rate is 1.5 x N$28 = N$42 an hour, so the overtime pay is 6 x N$42 = N$252, and gross pay for the week is N$1 120 + N$252 = N$1 372.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Time rates suit work where output cannot be counted cleanly or where quality matters more than speed - repairs, care work, skilled fitting. They are simple to calculate and easy for employees to check, and they give a predictable income, which answers the need for security. Because pay does not rise with output, there is no built-in reason to work faster, so businesses using time rates usually rely on supervision, and a poor worker and a good one on the same grade take home the same amount.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A salary is a fixed annual sum agreed with the employee and paid in equal instalments, usually monthly, regardless of the exact hours worked in any one period. A salary of N$276 000 a year is paid as N$276 000 / 12 = N$23 000 a month.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Salaries suit managerial, professional and administrative work, where the job is defined by responsibilities rather than by counted output and where hours vary from week to week. For the employee a salary gives a dependable income that can be planned around and a degree of standing; for the employer it makes the wage bill predictable and removes the administration of counting hours. The weakness is that nothing in the arrangement links pay to how much is achieved, so a salary is often combined with a bonus or a performance award.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A salary differs from time-based pay in what is being paid for. Time rates pay for hours counted, so extra hours bring extra pay and a short week brings less; a salary pays for a role, so the monthly amount is the same whether the month was busy or quiet, and additional hours usually bring no additional payment.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A piece rate pays an employee an agreed amount for each unit they produce or task they complete, so gross pay = units produced x rate per unit. Piece-rate schemes often include a guaranteed minimum payment so that an employee whose machine breaks down does not go unpaid.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A garment workshop in Oshakati pays N$6.50 for each finished shirt. A machinist who completes 420 shirts in a week earns 420 x N$6.50 = N$2 730 for that week. If a fault in the cutting room limits her to 180 shirts the following week, the same rate gives 180 x N$6.50 = N$1 170, which is why a guaranteed weekly minimum is usually written into the agreement.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Piece rates give the clearest possible link between effort and pay, and where the work is repetitive and each unit can be counted they tend to raise output quickly. The costs come with that link. Speed can be bought at the expense of quality and of safe working, so inspection has to be added and paid for; income becomes unstable when supplies or machinery fail, which undermines the employee's security; the method does not fit work done jointly by a team; and setting the rate is a recurring source of dispute, because a rate that becomes easy to beat costs the employer and one that is tightened is seen as a cut.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Commission pays an employee a percentage of the value of the sales they make, usually on top of a basic wage. Commission earned = value of sales x commission rate.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A vehicle salesperson in Swakopmund is paid a basic wage of N$4 000 a month plus 4% commission on the value of what she sells. In a month in which she sells N$186 000 of vehicles, commission is N$186 000 x 0.04 = N$7 440, so total pay is N$4 000 + N$7 440 = N$11 440. In a quiet month with N$60 000 of sales the commission falls to N$2 400 and total pay to N$6 400.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Commission suits selling roles where each sale can be attributed to one person, and it lets the business carry a lower fixed wage bill because much of the cost arises only when revenue does. Against that, a commission-only or commission-heavy package can push employees towards selling customers what earns most rather than what suits them, which can cost the business repeat trade; it fits badly where a sale is the work of several people or takes months to close; and earnings move with market conditions the salesperson does not control, so income in a downturn may fall below what the household needs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A bonus is a lump sum paid in addition to normal pay when a stated target is reached or a stated event occurs. Bonuses may be individual, awarded to a team, or paid across the whole workforce, and they may be tied to output, to attendance, to completing a contract on time or to the trading result of a year.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A construction firm promises a team of 8 site workers a shared bonus of N$96 000 for completing a school hall before the school year starts. The team finishes on time, so each member receives N$96 000 / 8 = N$12 000. The payment is a one-off addition to the wages already earned, and the firm is not committed to repeating it on the next contract.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A bonus concentrates effort on one stated result within a stated period, and because it is a one-off the employer takes on no permanent addition to the wage bill. Its weaknesses follow from the same features. A target the employees regard as out of reach produces very little effort, because the expectation that effort will earn the payment is what makes the offer work at all. A bonus repeated every year tends to become an expected part of pay, so its withdrawal causes more resentment than its payment produced enthusiasm. And a bonus tied to one measure draws attention away from what is not measured, such as safe working on a site under time pressure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A bonus and performance-related pay are not the same arrangement. A bonus is a lump sum triggered by a stated target or event and carries no commitment beyond that occasion. Performance-related pay follows an assessment of how an individual has performed against agreed objectives over a period, and the award may be added permanently to basic pay rather than paid once.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profit sharing distributes an agreed share of the business's profit to employees, usually as a stated percentage of profit divided between them or as a percentage of each person's own pay. The payment depends on the result the business achieves and is made after that result is known.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A food processor earning a profit of N$4 200 000 shares 5% of it among 60 employees. The pool is N$4 200 000 x 0.05 = N$210 000, and an equal division gives N$210 000 / 60 = N$3 500 each. In a year when profit falls to N$1 200 000 the same rule gives a pool of N$60 000 and N$1 000 each, and in a loss-making year it gives nothing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profit sharing lines employees' interests up with the trading result, so waste, avoidable cost and lost sales become their concern as well as management's, and it can build a sense of being part of the business rather than merely employed by it. The difficulty is the weakness of the link for any one person: an individual's extra effort makes almost no visible difference to a company-wide profit figure, the figure also moves with prices, exchange rates and demand that employees do not control, the payment arrives long after the effort, and in a poor year the reward disappears at exactly the moment employees feel least secure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Performance-related pay awards extra pay to an individual on the basis of an assessment of their performance against objectives agreed in advance. The award may be a one-off payment or an increase to basic pay, and the assessment is normally made by a manager at a review meeting held at set intervals.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An insurance company in Windhoek pays a claims handler a basic salary of N$18 000 a month and operates three performance bands worth 2%, 4% and 6% of basic pay. A handler placed in the top band receives an extra N$18 000 x 0.06 = N$1 080 a month, while one placed in the lowest band receives N$360. The gap between the bands is N$720 a month, and whether that gap is large enough to change how the work is done is the question the company has to answer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Performance-related pay extends the idea of paying for results into work whose output cannot be counted in units, which is most office and service work. Setting objectives in advance forces a conversation about what the job is actually for, the review gives the employee feedback they might not otherwise receive, and a visible reward for strong performance helps retain the people a business least wants to lose.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The scheme depends entirely on the assessment being accurate and seen to be fair, and where employees regard a manager's judgement as arbitrary the effect on effort can be negative. Rewarding individuals can weaken cooperation, because time spent helping a colleague does not appear in one's own assessment. Objectives that can be measured tend to crowd out the parts of a job that cannot. And the sums involved are often small relative to basic pay, so the scheme may cost management time out of proportion to the change in behaviour it produces.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Fringe benefits are rewards given in addition to wages or salary rather than as cash pay - a company vehicle, a housing or transport allowance, medical aid, employer pension contributions, subsidised meals, staff discount or paid study leave. They are sometimes called perks.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Fringe benefits help a business attract and keep employees, and they reach needs that a wage reaches only indirectly: medical aid and a pension answer security, a vehicle or a reserved office answers standing. Some can be provided more cheaply by the employer than the employee could buy them, which makes the package worth more than its cost. The limits are that employees value them very differently, so a benefit one person regards as decisive another regards as worthless; they cost money whether or not they change behaviour; they become an expected entitlement that is difficult to withdraw; and their tax treatment depends on the jurisdiction, which affects what they are actually worth.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A fringe benefit differs from pay in that it is received in a particular form rather than as money the employee can spend as they choose. That is its strength and its weakness: it can meet a need the employee might not have spent cash on, such as a pension, but an employee who has no use for the particular benefit gains nothing from it, where the equivalent cash would have been worth its full amount to them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A non-financial motivator is a reward that comes from the work itself or from the employee's position and treatment in the organisation rather than from the money paid. The forms named in this syllabus are training, opportunities for promotion, development, status, job re-design, team working, empowerment, participation and job enrichment.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Non-financial motivators work on the needs that money reaches poorly. Once pay is at a level the employee regards as adequate, further money answers a need that is already largely met, while recognition, responsibility and the chance to grow answer needs that are not. This is the practical content of Herzberg's distinction between removing dissatisfaction and producing positive motivation, and of Maslow's point that a satisfied need loses its power to motivate.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Non-financial motivators are not free. Training costs fees and lost working time, job re-design costs management time and may need new equipment, and participation costs the hours people spend in meetings. They also work poorly where a more basic need is unmet: enriching the job of an employee whose wage does not cover their household's costs is likely to change little. They are better understood as methods that answer different needs from pay than as a cheaper substitute for it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training is planned instruction that gives an employee the knowledge and skills their job requires - induction training on joining, on-the-job training alongside an experienced worker, and off-the-job training away from the workplace such as a course or a supplier's programme.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training motivates through two routes. It raises the employee's competence, so work that was difficult becomes manageable and the employee can reasonably expect their effort to produce the required result - the expectancy element in Vroom's theory. And the business spending money on a person signals that it values them and intends to keep them, which answers esteem and security needs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training has to be paid for in fees and in the output lost while the employee is away, and a better-trained employee becomes more attractive to other employers, so some of the benefit may leave with them. Its motivating effect also depends on what follows: where the new skills are never used, or where the course is understood as something the business is obliged to run, the training is unlikely to change effort at all.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training and development are distinguished by their horizon. Training equips an employee for the job they hold now and is judged by whether they can do it better. Development builds a person's capability over a longer period and for roles they do not yet hold, and is judged by what they become able to take on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Promotion, in this topic, means advancing an employee to a post of higher rank carrying greater responsibility and usually higher pay. The word has an unrelated meaning in marketing, where promotion means the communication a business uses to persuade customers to buy; the two senses share nothing but the word.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The prospect of promotion motivates where employees can see a route upwards, understand what performance is needed to travel it, and believe that posts genuinely become available. It answers esteem needs through the recognition a higher rank carries, and it answers the need to grow through the wider work the post involves.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Promotion as a motivator depends on there being somewhere to promote people to. A small business with a flat structure may have no vacancy for years, in which case dangling the prospect produces disappointment rather than effort. Promotion also has costs of its own: for every employee promoted others were not, and their reaction may offset the gain; and a business that promotes its best technician into management can lose a good technician and gain a weak manager, because the two jobs call for different abilities.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Development is the longer-term growth of an employee's capability beyond the demands of their present job - through mentoring, moving across departments to widen experience, studying for a professional qualification, or leading a project that stretches them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Development motivates because it treats the employee as a person with a future rather than as a holder of a post. It answers the need to grow and use one's abilities, it makes an internal promotion realistic and so gives the promotion route credibility, and it tends to hold ambitious employees who would otherwise look elsewhere for a bigger job.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Development takes years to show a return and costs money and senior time before it shows anything, which makes it vulnerable when a business is under financial pressure. It can also raise expectations that the business is then unable to meet: an employee who has completed a qualification and finds no larger role waiting may leave sooner than if nothing had been offered.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Status is the standing an employee holds relative to others in the organisation, together with the visible markers that signal it - a job title, a uniform or badge, an office rather than a shared desk, a reserved parking space, or a seat on a committee.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Status answers the need for respect from others and for self-respect, which is the esteem level of Maslow's hierarchy and sits among Herzberg's motivators as a form of recognition. It is also cheap relative to pay, which is why a business that cannot afford a large increase can still change how valued an employee feels.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Status depends on other people recognising the marker, so it works where colleagues and customers read the title or the badge as meaning something and does little where they do not. Markers that separate employees can breed resentment among those who do not have them. And a title given without any change in responsibility tends to be seen through, after which it carries less weight than before it was given.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Job re-design means deliberately changing the content or structure of a job to make it more satisfying and to raise the effort employees are willing to give. It is an umbrella term covering job rotation, job enlargement and job enrichment.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The three forms of job re-design differ in what they change. Job rotation moves an employee between tasks of similar difficulty at planned intervals, so the variety changes while the level of responsibility does not. Job enlargement adds further tasks at the same level, widening the job horizontally. Job enrichment adds responsibility, decision-making and a complete unit of work, deepening the job vertically.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Job re-design attacks boredom at its source, which is the narrowness of the work rather than the conditions around it. Rotation also makes a workforce more flexible, because employees who have worked several positions can cover absence, and it reduces the risk of repetitive strain from doing one movement all day.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Re-design costs management time to plan and usually needs training before employees can move between tasks, and output may dip while people learn. Widening a job that remains dull can be experienced as more of the same work rather than better work, and employees who are content with a familiar routine may resist the change. Where the re-design is introduced without consultation it can be read as a way of extracting more work for the same pay.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Team working organises employees into groups that are jointly responsible for a complete task or area of work, with the group deciding between its members how the work is allocated and often setting its own working arrangements within limits set by management.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Team working answers the need to belong, which is the social level of Maslow's hierarchy and the central point of Mayo's human relations school. Members support each other, cover absence, and pass on skills without a formal course, and the wish not to let colleagues down can raise effort in a way no supervisor achieves.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The group's own standard of a reasonable day's work can sit below what management wants as easily as above it, and an individual whose effort is hidden inside a group result may coast on the work of others. Teams take longer to reach decisions than one person does, personal conflict inside a small group is hard to escape, and work that is genuinely individual gains little from being organised this way.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Empowerment gives employees the authority to make decisions about their own work without referring them upwards, together with the information and resources to decide well and accountability for the results.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Empowerment motivates by supplying responsibility and control, which are among Herzberg's motivators and reach the esteem and self-actualisation levels of Maslow's hierarchy. It also improves the work itself: the person closest to a problem usually knows most about it, and a decision taken on the spot reaches the customer faster than one referred through two levels of management.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Empowerment works where the boundaries of the authority are stated, the employee has been trained and given the information a good decision needs, and managers accept the decisions that come back. Where a manager reverses those decisions the arrangement is empowerment in name only and tends to leave employees more cynical than before. Some employees experience the added responsibility as pressure rather than reward, and a mistake made by an employee acting within their authority still costs the business money.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Empowerment and participation differ in who finally decides. Participation gives employees a voice in a decision that someone else takes; empowerment transfers the decision itself, within stated limits, to the employee doing the work.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Participation means involving employees in decisions that affect their work, through consultation meetings, team briefings, suggestion schemes, joint committees and employee representation, so that their views are heard before a decision is taken.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Participation motivates because being asked signals that the employee's judgement is valued, which answers esteem needs, and because people who have helped shape a decision tend to accept it more readily than people to whom it is announced. That acceptance matters most when the decision involves a change to how work is done.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Consultation takes time and slows decisions down, which is costly where a situation is urgent. Its motivating effect depends on employees seeing that what they said made a difference: where the same proposals are consulted on and nothing ever changes, participation is read as a formality and can leave employees more cynical than no consultation at all. Employees may also lack the information needed to contribute usefully to decisions that reach beyond their own work.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Job enrichment gives an employee a complete and identifiable piece of work, the responsibility and authority to decide how it is carried out, and direct feedback on the result. It deepens a job vertically by adding decisions that a manager previously took.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Job enrichment is distinguished from job enlargement by the direction of the change. Enlargement adds more tasks at the same level, so the employee does more things of the kind they already did. Enrichment adds responsibility and decision-making, so the employee does the same work with greater control over it and is answerable for the outcome.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Enrichment is the practical form of Herzberg's argument, and where it works the reward is built into the job and does not have to be paid for again each period. It requires training, because an employee handed decisions they have not been prepared for may make poor ones; it takes authority away from supervisors, who may resist it; and employees may reasonably ask for more pay for work that now carries more responsibility, so a method presented as an alternative to higher wages can end up raising them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Employee participation in the management and control of a business means arrangements that give employees a share in decisions beyond their own immediate task - about how a department is run, how the business responds to a change, and in some forms about the direction of the business itself.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The usual arrangements, in rising order of how much say they give, are: team briefings and consultation meetings, which inform employees and invite comment; suggestion schemes, which collect proposals and often pay for those adopted; quality circles, small voluntary groups that meet regularly to identify and solve problems in their own area of work; works councils or joint consultative committees, standing bodies of elected employee representatives that management must consult on stated matters; employee representatives or worker directors sitting on the board; and employee share ownership, which makes employees part-owners with the voting rights that go with shares.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: These arrangements form a ladder rather than a list, and the rungs are being informed, being consulted, deciding jointly, and owning. A team briefing that only passes information down gives no say at all; a works council with a right to be consulted gives a say without the final word; a worker director takes part in the decision; and a shareholding employee holds a share of control permanently, through votes, alongside a share of the reward, through dividends.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Participation in management can improve the decisions themselves, because employees doing the work often see problems and remedies that managers do not, and a quality circle turns that knowledge into proposals that can be costed. It also tends to reduce resistance to change, because employees who were consulted about a new method understand why it is being introduced. And it answers esteem and self-actualisation needs, which is why it appears in this topic rather than only in a discussion of organisation.

claims.text: Participation slows decisions, which is a real cost when a business has to respond quickly. Employees may not have the commercial information to judge a strategic question, and some matters cannot be discussed widely without harming the business. Managers may resist arrangements that reduce their authority, or may run them as a formality, and where employees see that consultation changes nothing the arrangement damages trust rather than building it. Employee shareholders may also find their savings and their job exposed to the same business, which concentrates their risk.

claims.text: Participation is more likely to repay its cost where managers act on what comes back and are seen to, where employees have enough information to contribute usefully, where the matters put to them are ones they know something about, and where the business is not facing a decision so urgent that consultation would arrive too late. Where those conditions are absent, the same arrangements can consume time and produce cynicism.

claims.text: It is a mistake to conclude from Herzberg that pay does not motivate. The theory's claim is narrower: correcting pay removes a reason for dissatisfaction without by itself producing positive effort, and where pay is below what an employee needs to live on it behaves quite differently, because the need it answers is still pressing.

claims.text: It is a mistake to treat non-financial motivators as the cheap option. Training, job re-design and consultation all consume money and management time, and they address different needs from pay rather than substituting for it, so a business that cuts wages and offers recognition instead is likely to find effort falling rather than rising.

claims.text: It is a mistake to assume that a method which motivated one workforce will motivate another. What a reward is worth depends on the needs of the people offered it, so the same scheme may work well in one department and do nothing in the next, and the test of any scheme is what happens to the figures the business chose to watch.
